scores.notes: The piece leans so hard on what it can't prove, repeating the same caveats and the 2→9→1 page counts in nearly every section, that the strong contrast between the second and third rewrites gets diluted. It also invents claims the author never made, such as pages being 'customer evidence' and the 'noise from a new system settling in' rationale.

The post says the 40,000 rows were lost in the second incident and that `--rename-map` answers the rename questions ahead of time; the author answers support neither claim, and there is no command example or sample output to show how tidepool works.

The material is strong, but the piece leans on repeated not-X-but-Y turns and tidy one-line section closers, and its ending lesson ('put the lunch on the calendar the day you cancel') feels pre-packaged rather than earned.

The angle is the stock small-room plant post, 'pick the right plants for your light,' and the author's sharpest details, the landlord's remark and the per-plant watering log, are reported flatly instead of carrying the piece.

The piece repeats the same three numbers four or five times and stacks on meta-commentary ('its shortness is the point', 'I don't think that's a coincidence', the 'common version of this post' setup), so a thin story gets padded to essay length when it needs more scene detail.

The middle section explains a point HN readers already accept (renames are ambiguous) and never shows the actual prompt or a sample `--rename-map` file, so it leans on story instead of showing the tool.

The piece leans heavily on disclaimers like 「我說不準」「老實說」 and on lines that just restate the author's answers, so the 'who pays the cost' angle feels thin. The closing three-item list and the not-X-but-Y framing also feel formulaic.

The piece lists every author fact as a tidy how-to, with no felt moment or specific failure story, and it invents details to fill the gaps: the landlord pausing at the door, the rod needing no drilled holes, and no longer having to replace pots.
